source.title: The Forgotten Economists
source.summary: A 1,500-year journey through Islamic economic thought: from Mecca to Ibn Khaldun to the modern revival.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Did you know that a 14th-century Muslim scholar described supply and demand, the division of labor, and the labor theory of value, four hundred years before Adam Smith? In this pilot episode, we trace the entire arc of Islamic economic thought: from the bustling markets of pre-Islamic Mecca and the Prophet Muhammad's career as a merchant, through the golden age of scholars like Abu Yusuf, Al-Ghazali, and Ibn Khaldun, to the colonial disruption and the remarkable modern revival of Islamic finance.

x.single_post: Ibn Khaldun described supply and demand, division of labor, and the labor theory of value in the 14th century. Why did we wait 400 years to call Adam Smith the father of economics?
thread: Ibn Khaldun described supply and demand, division of labor, and the labor theory of value in the 14th century. Adam Smith wouldn't be born for another 400 years.
Before him came Abu Yusuf and Al-Ghazali. Before them, the Prophet Muhammad worked as a merchant in the bustling markets of pre-Islamic Mecca.
Islamic economic thought had a golden age that lasted centuries. Then came colonial disruption, and the tradition went underground.
Today there's a remarkable revival happening. The forgotten economists are being remembered. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1

linkedin.post: Ibn Khaldun described supply and demand, division of labor, and the labor theory of value in the 14th century. Adam Smith wouldn't arrive for another 400 years. The story of Islamic economic thought spans 1,500 years: from the Prophet Muhammad's career as a merchant in pre-Islamic Mecca, through the golden age of Abu Yusuf and Al-Ghazali, to Ibn Khaldun's sophisticated analysis, then colonial disruption and a remarkable modern revival. These weren't abstract theorists. They were practitioners writing from within thriving commercial civilizations, developing frameworks that balanced spiritual values with economic reality. Why did this tradition disappear from mainstream economic history? And what can we learn from its revival today? Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-1
